sourceStates.title: [skyrl] Match upstream vLLM's NCCL algorithm selection
sourceStates.body:
Set SkyRL's learner `NCCL_ALGO` to `ring,tree;allreduce:tree`, matching [upstream vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58179) and [the companion vLLM change](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/139). The learner and vLLM share a weight-publication group and should use the same NCCL settings.

The previous `ring;allreduce:tree` value selects the same algorithms with NCCL 2.32.6: [Tree is only implemented for AllReduce](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl/blob/v2.32.6-1/src/device/generate.py#L104-L112), which both values pin to Tree. This follows up on #11956 to use the exact upstream setting. No new tests were run.

sourceStates.title: [skyrl] Adopt the vLLM wheel with batch-invariant NCCL algorithms
sourceStates.body:
SkyRL installs a vLLM wheel whose batch-invariant mode keeps NCCL's Ring and Tree algorithms enabled, so vLLM engine processes can run AllGather under NCCL 2.32.6. The wheel is [marin-vllm-gpu-20261124-7e9b413a5daf](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261124-7e9b413a5daf); its initializer sets `NCCL_ALGO=ring,tree;allreduce:tree` (marin-community/vllm#139), the value SkyRL's learner and Ray workers use, so the learner takes the value from the initializer. The previous wheel's initializer set `NCCL_ALGO=allreduce:tree`, which leaves AllGather without an algorithm under NCCL 2.32.6, and the GPU nightly's disaggregated rollout test failed with `NCCL error: invalid usage`.

The wheel also carries the fork's GrugMoE and speculative-decoding changes since the previous pin: full decode graphs and GB200 expert GEMM tuning, Triton MoE workspace reservation, padding-logit clearing before expert selection, ShortConv output writes, dense speculative drafts kept out of expert-parallel groups, and DSpark serving for Grug drafts. The release passed the fork's H100 and GB200 wheel qualification. In `vendor/skyrl/uv.lock` only the `vllm` entries change, and `uv lock --check` passes.

The [SkyRL GPU nightly on this branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/45365513133) passed all three H100 lanes, including the Grug Megatron suite and its disaggregated rollout test. sourceStates.title: [rl] Bound PPO vocabulary memory before rollout admission
sourceStates.body:
Long packed trajectories can exhaust trainer memory after rollouts finish: PPO materializes a full token-by-vocabulary output projection and its backward. Add two opt-in Megatron policy options, both absent from resolved recipes until a recipe sets them, so existing launch identities stay unchanged.

`output_projection_chunk_size` computes token log-probs and entropy through a token-chunked projection with a recomputed backward and native gradient accumulation, instead of a full vocabulary tensor (TP1 PPO without sequence parallelism). `memory_profile` runs a warm-Adam capacity check on every policy rank before initial weight publication and rollout admission: it initializes the optimizer, measures forward, backward and optimizer steps at each configured token count plus `trainer.algorithm.max_seq_len`, and requires a configured device-memory headroom fraction. Sizing restores model, master shards, optimizer, scheduler and random state afterwards, and an enabled check requires explicit capacity and headroom.

sourceStates.title: [evals] Grade GPQA Diamond on final answers only
sourceStates.body:
`gpqa-diamond` (198 questions from [`Idavidrein/gpqa`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Idavidrein/gpqa) at `83022cef`, Evalchemy prompt, 3 trials) used the default `combine` response selection, so the letter extractor read the reasoning and final answer together. A `\boxed{X}` written mid-reasoning could be scored as the answer, and unclosed reasoning could still score. This switches GPQA items to `response_selection="final_only"`, matching the other curated generation evals, and gives GPQA its own protocol version (`2026.11.21`) so new scores are not pooled with earlier `gpqa-diamond` records. MMLU-Pro shares the item builder in the Evalchemy importer (from #10957) and keeps its protocol (`2026.11.02`) and selection. GPQA data is CC-BY-4.0 and gated.

Full runs on cw-rno2a, 594 attempts each (198 × 3), exact-letter grading:

| Model | Hardware | Graded | Accuracy | Empty or truncated answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | H100x2 | 594/594 | 84.7 ± 2.2 | 0 |
| Snowball v0.1 (`reasoning_parser: grug`) | H100x8 | 594/594 | 63.8 ± 2.9 | 4 empty (answer left in reasoning) |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | H100x4 | 546/594 | 91.2 ± 2.0 on graded; 83.8 counting missing as wrong | 14 hit the context limit |

Every Glimmer answer is a single `\boxed{X}`, and reasoning comes back separately in turn metadata, so `final_only` grades only the answer. On 10 attempts Snowball boxed the option's value instead of its letter (`\boxed{18}` for D); these score 0 under the prompt's letter-only instruction. The Nemotron run did not finish: on 19 questions its reasoning ran past the 1,800 s per-request cap (`EVALUATION_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), 194 of its 213 timeouts. GPQA sets no output-token limit. The next Nemotron run will cap its context or output; that is deferred, not in this PR.

sourceStates.title: [rl] Refresh Snowball controls and reduce train-long memory
sourceStates.body:
Snowball's gated presets compare candidates against controls collected at each preset's current revision. Speed-short, data-short and speed-medium ran from a main checkout with a one-line change to request production priority. Speed-long and learning-medium ran this branch's rendezvous fix at `2b454ac4b4` with the same priority setting. Learning-medium and data-medium share the Reno cohort at `2026.11.20.4`. The four other pinned presets use `2026.11.20.3`. The gate checks every control's stored launch configuration against the current preset defaults. It validates model and tokenizer cache paths against their declared sources, resolves the pinned output paths, and estimates GPU-hours from first workload start to native completion.

Control cohorts keep every completed, measured run. The six learning-medium EvalLite family means are 0.6285, 0.6116, 0.6101, 0.6098, 0.6033, and 0.5925. The five speed-long median update times are 80.55, 80.09, 81.15, 79.97, and 84.60 seconds. The 84.60-second speed-long run exceeds its leave-one-out tolerance and contributes to the calibration.

A control pin can identify its collection cluster. The gate resolves that cluster’s stored controls and validates them against native defaults for the collection placement. Candidates retain their preset placement.

Multi-node NCCL validation scopes each rendezvous to its native Iris job and attempt. Concurrent Snowball replicas can each validate their own ranks in one coordinator namespace.

RL launches read published task selections as immutable inputs using `ArtifactStep.adopt(..., read_only=True)` in `marin.execution`. The coordinator resolves their original paths and fingerprints while the selection producer owns the metadata and status files.

A Snowball train-long run exhausted GPU memory while allocating a 4.97 GiB softmax gradient. The `2026.11.21.2` preset splits each packed policy sequence across two Megatron context ranks and gathers keys and values for sliding-window attention. It uses 40 H100s with a 24,576-token context and an 8,192-token reply limit. A 25-update proof on 40 H100s passed the original failure point and graded all 100 EvalLite tasks at updates 0, 10, 20 and 25. The proof ran with Hugging Face export disabled. [Proof run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin-snowball-rl/runs/ad32076d128a)

`train-long` is the only preset whose launch configuration changes, and the native revision test confirms that every other Snowball and Mochi preset retains its revision and fingerprint.

diagnostics.title: Measure final Mochi and Gemma 4 31B on July code to estimate Mochi’s base-model perplexity
diagnostics.body:
Prompted by Calvin Xu @Calvin-Xu 

Where would the final Mochi base model land on the base-model log-perplexity plot shared by Elie Bakouch? We can measure how well Mochi predicts public code and use open models that appear on the plot to estimate its position. The estimate inherits uncertainty because the public code and the plot use different evaluation data. [Original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972) · [OpenAI evaluation](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/) · [Earlier Marin PPL comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8824)

### Estimated position on the original plot

![Elie Bakouch’s full comparison chart with the final Mochi estimate marked as an orange star.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/e5a6e3d019f9efd4cf8089daded2cbf45af3c179/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/mochi-final-placement.png)

Elie Bakouch’s original figure includes the OpenAI series, MAI-1 and MAI-2 Base, the green MAI-paper comparisons, and the purple Inkling comparisons with their calibration ranges. The orange star adds Mochi at its November 17 release date. Its height (0.879) comes from our separate July-code calibration using DeepSeek V4 Pro Base, Kimi K2 Base, and Gemma 4 31B. [Original figure and method by Elie Bakouch](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972)

### Direct measurement

Score the released **Mochi base checkpoint at step 393,491** and **Gemma 4 31B base** on the same 500 C++ files and 500 Python files from July 2026 UncheatableEval. Both Iris runs use 4,096-token windows and each model’s native tokenizer. For each language, sum the prediction loss across all tokens and divide by the total number of UTF-8 bytes. Report bits per byte (lower is better), then give the two languages equal weight in the comparison. [Pinned dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07/tree/65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545) · [Mochi checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Mochi-535B-A23B/tree/c8bb74061a11f21bc4b432e498060e2cb199e40c) · [Gemma checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B/tree/5bbc2fb1c1b2c611d06e3d9f23c170ba21659d89)

### Results to record

- [x] Report direct C++ and Python bits per byte for both models.
- [x] Compare our Gemma scores with its published July results (0.25293 C++, 0.33209 Python) to quantify the effect of scoring settings.
- [x] Report the estimated Mochi plot coordinate with two anchors and with Gemma included. Show how much the choice changes the answer.

### Direct July results

Both Iris runs completed. Each row uses the same 500 C++ and 500 Python files at a 4,096-token scoring window. Lower bits per byte mean better prediction.

| Base model | C++ | Python | Mean of languages |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Mochi, final step 393,491 | 0.22355 | 0.29184 | 0.25769 |
| Gemma 4 31B | 0.25293 | 0.33205 | 0.29249 |

![Direct July C++ and Python bits per byte for Mochi and three open models. Mochi falls between DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base on both.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/126400d006cf2d8e012ba2aa73647428f237d879/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/july-code-scores.png)

Mochi lands between DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base in both languages. DeepSeek and Kimi use Marin’s archived July measurements.

The Gemma rerun is within 0.00005 bits/byte of the published score in each language. For Mochi, DeepSeek and Kimi give an estimated chart coordinate of **0.8788**. Including Gemma gives **0.8795**. When held out, Gemma's estimated chart height misses its inferred reference by **0.0103**. The two Mochi estimates agreeing within 0.0007 therefore understates the uncertainty in translating public code loss to OpenAI’s evaluation. [Public July data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07) · [Code-to-chart calibration sources](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf)

### Contamination check

**Confirmed code-bearing overlap in 19 July files (10 C++, 9 Python).** The matching passages range from common scaffolding and generated code to a vendored TinyXML implementation. One 4,096-token training sequence at step 150,417 contains 1,174 consecutive tokens from the scored July file, including string encoding and XML node operations. The July repository reused code that Mochi had already seen. [Pinned July file](https://github.com/takagi-ryo-ac/RTSS/blob/86a93eaaeff19ccca78272a183028154536bea29/tinyxml.cpp)

| Example | Consecutive tokens in a single training sequence | Zero-based training step |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TinyXML library implementation, C++ | 1,174 of 2,518 scored tokens | 150,417 |
| Alembic online/offline migration template, Python | 278 of 546 | 220,782 |
| Qt-generated meta-object code, C++ | 167 of 1,152 | 150,985 |
| Dear ImGui Win32/OpenGL example, C++ | 91 of 2,017 | 177,190 |

**Audit method.** We sampled 15,872 distinct blocks from 16 code-heavy training-data buckets during steps 146,355–231,664. All 16,642,998,272 sampled tokens came from shuffle windows fully consumed by that run. We searched for 48-token exact matches, starting every 16 test tokens and requiring at least 12 identifier, operator or keyword positions outside strings and comments. We extended each match to its exact boundaries. For each of the 19 files, we replayed a witness through the pinned training loader and independently reread its bytes from the training store. Two Qt-generated files and one Alembic template account for 365 of the 404 match occurrences. A file can occur repeatedly. [Recorded training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k) · [Pinned data loader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ad754c6d67555d6369a4a312ff7388e43cfd08c1/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/dataset.py)

**Effect on the comparison.** Both models are rescored from their stored per-file losses on the same retained files. The gap is Gemma BPB minus Mochi BPB. Positive values favor Mochi.

| July files retained | C++ files | C++ gap | Python files | Python gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All | 500 | 0.02939 | 500 | 0.04021 |
| Exclude the 19 files with verified code overlap | 490 | 0.02923 | 491 | 0.03991 |
| Exclude entire files with obvious license or copyright markers | 465 | 0.02611 | 483 | 0.03981 |
| Exclude the union of those sets and earlier flagged files | 453 | 0.02536 | 473 | 0.03903 |

The 19 confirmed files establish a lower bound. Most training tokens were outside the scan, and edited copies can evade exact matching. The public-code comparison with Gemma survives every exclusion above. The 0.879 chart estimate still uses the full July data, since matching per-file scores for DeepSeek and Kimi are needed to recalibrate the filtered comparison.

#### Earlier license and training-pool checks


Marin's training-time decontamination corpus omitted UncheatableEval. The benchmark’s GitHub crawler filters by repository creation date, samples a file, and records the repository push date. Old code and licenses can occur in a new repository. [Marin decontamination audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10541) · [July crawler](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval/blob/bf068ff0863f1f3398b20a8ae64f50c29765e860/crawlers/crawler/spiders/github.py#L112)

A targeted scan of 201,326,592 tokens in the final run’s Harrier data store found exact passages in three July files. For two, I reconstructed the training batch with the recorded run configuration and the pinned Levanter forward loader, then fetched the tokens at that position and compared them with the scored July file. Both verified passages are license/header text.

| July test row (zero-based) | Language | Exact consecutive tokens | Training step (zero-based) |
| ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4221 | C++ | 206 | 145,950 |
| 6200 | Python | 118 | 167,299 |

The third match was another license header (142 C++ tokens) in the training pool. Separately, at least three July files contain identifiable implementation code that predates August 2025, including Dear ImGui and urllib3. That date check establishes reuse of old code. The fraction of all July files seen during training remains unknown. [C++ training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-main-step121638) · [Python training run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k) · [Training data order](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ad754c6d67555d6369a4a312ff7388e43cfd08c1/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/dataset.py) · [Official Stack v3 snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceCode/stack-v3-train)

An additional targeted scan of **1,609,826,304 training tokens** found zero exact 96-token matches that contained at least 16 identifier, operator or keyword positions outside strings and comments. This sample leaves most of the training stream unexamined. Removing all eight July files flagged by either the store or old-source checks leaves Mochi at **0.22560 C++ / 0.29255 Python**, versus **0.25346 / 0.33236** for Gemma on those same files.

### Newer official holdout candidate

As of November 23, the latest public UncheatableEval release is **2026-10**. Its standard test split contains 500 C++ and 500 Python files with recorded repository push dates of October 1–22. The final Mochi run's nonzero training components point to the August Harrier store. October is a useful temporal separation for genuinely new code, although recently created repositories can carry older files. [Official release collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/Jellyfish042/uncheatableeval) · [Pinned October data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-10/tree/87a300906c15c2433c5285035042dabdcbec0725) · [Final Mochi training configuration](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-lce-log65536sq-step390k)

**Screened October split for a larger comparison.** The same 16.643B consumed-training-token scan found code-bearing matches in 18 C++ and 3 Python files. For all 21 files we replayed a witness using the pinned loader and independently reread the corresponding training bytes. Removing those files, obvious vendored/generated files, and near duplicates of July or an already retained October file leaves **470 C++ and 490 Python files**. Retained files use the official scored text byte-for-byte. Residual train overlap is possible outside the audited sample and for edited copies. All comparison models need scores on these same retained files.

<details>
<summary>Reproduce the 960-file split from the pinned October Parquet</summary>

Read the original test Parquet in order, select the categories `github_cpp` and `github_python`, and exclude these zero-based row indices from the original 7,500-row table. The SHA-256 of the upstream Parquet is `bf8a59a3b4a248bfcb1af454594e83a39eee129340e049a11784a2536840748f`.

`4001, 4004, 4022, 4031, 4033, 4044, 4047, 4051, 4085, 4098, 4101, 4115, 4124, 4163, 4166, 4185, 4188, 4214, 4241, 4244, 4249, 4272, 4358, 4363, 4370, 4393, 4424, 4433, 4441, 4481, 6097, 6126, 6132, 6166, 6262, 6269, 6324, 6375, 6481, 6493`

The near-duplicate screen uses 13-token shingles with comments and whitespace removed and literals normalized. It excludes a candidate when at least 50% of its distinct shingles match one prior file and it contains at least 20 distinct shingles.

</details>

**Post-release cross-check.** We scanned the 22 November pilot files against the same 16.643B training tokens and found zero qualifying exact code matches. That small set is best used to check whether the October result transfers to files added after the checkpoint release.

### Post-release holdout pilot

The pilot retains **15 C++ files and 7 Python files from 22 repositories**, with one file per repository. Each corresponding pull request opened and merged November 18–22, after the November 17 Mochi release. The sample uses added files, pins each Git blob, and removes leading license headers from the scored text. [Mochi release](https://openathena.ai/blog/marin-mochi-pretraining-checkpoints/)

We screened for copied passages within the pilot, against the July benchmark, and against nearby files from the same repositories before release. A targeted scan of 201,326,592 Mochi training tokens found zero exact 96-token matches to the retained scored text. This small pilot provides examples for a fresher evaluation. diagnostics.title: [rl] Name the Mochi RL feature gaps between main presets and the long loop
diagnostics.body:
The Mochi RL presets in `experiments/post_training/mochi_rl.py` cannot yet reproduce what the long-loop runs on `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype`. An outside group that wants to do RL on the open Mochi model through main's preset entry point would hit the gaps below. This issue names the gaps only. How to implement them is the RL loop owners' call. @atqamar

Training-correctness fixes go up separately as standalone PRs and are not tracked here.

Gaps:
1. **No output model.** The presets set `checkpoints="none"` and `export="none"`. The long loop keeps improved eligible validation checkpoints, selects the best-by-validation checkpoint, keeps native checkpoints in permanent storage, and exports the final checkpoint to Hugging Face.
2. **Model input is an internal object-store path.** The presets adopt the SFT export from S3. Parity needs the published Mochi Hugging Face repository as input, with a pinned tokenizer and staged snapshot.
3. **Rollout scheduling defaults.** Main uses `full_batch` admission. The long loop defaults to rolling batches within curriculum route quotas, plus priority evaluation drain (abort, requeue, and fence before the next learner batch).
4. **Normalized RL configuration.** The long loop takes staleness and context limits from Mochi, and batch, clip and learning rate from Snowball. Main's presets differ.
5. **Curriculum.** The long loop's curriculum (`lib/marin/rl/curriculum.py`) owns a random ~200-prompt validation holdout taken out of train, derives route quotas, and samples by domain. Main can train only on a fixed selection such as `snowball-100k`.
6. **Placement.** Excluding faulty NVLink domains from Mochi placement depends on the controller change in #11948.
7. **Wall-clock budget.** The long loop gives RL a fixed 12-hour budget with a drain margin, shared with the Snowball control.
8. **Agentic paths after #12167.** Harbor-specific long-loop fixes (verdict retention, empty actions under behavior-logprob checks, judge credential relay) target code that #12167 removes. The RolloutEngine path needs equivalent behavior; the burn-down list is #12190.

Optional for parity: Megatron save-plan reuse and overlapping validation with checkpoint saves; request-timing and consumption telemetry; the Daytona snapshot pool; the hosted OpenResearcher retrieval service; Micro210 evaluation (#12069) to compare results.

Done when:
A `train-long` Mochi preset on main, started from the published Mochi model, trains on a curriculum with a holdout, uses the long-loop scheduling and configuration defaults, and exports the best-by-validation checkpoint to Hugging Face.

diagnostics.title: [verifyit] Compound units, ordinals and signed unit powers misgrade since #11989
diagnostics.body:
Since #11989 (e3de9706b), three shapes of math reference no longer grade as they did before it. Each is either rejected at conversion, which drops its row, or parsed with part of its text as a symbol, so the right value scores 0. A census of every row of the `MarinSkyRL` math sources and the five TaskTrove math sets (the method of [my review on #11989](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11989#issuecomment-7113679024)) finds 27 such rows: `numina_math` 24, `deepscaler` 3. Before #11989 (0c236d36c), each of these references gave 1 to its value and 0 to the value raised by one.

| Shape | Rows | Examples | On e3de9706b |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Compound unit | 12 | `\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}`, `215 \, \text{kJ}/\text{mol}`, `30 \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}` | 10 rejected; in 2 (`30 \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}`, `1.8^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{h}`) the value scores 0 |
| Ordinal | 14 | `11^{\text{th}}`, `25^{\text{th}}`, `4^{\text{th}} \text{ minute}` | the number scores 0 |
| Unit power with a sign or spaces | 1 | `9.9 \, \text{s}^{-1}` (also `15\mbox{ cm}^{ 2 }`) | rejected |

Causes, all in `_parse_reference` of `lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py`:

- Compound units: the tail check ([L129](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e3de9706b774c02117ec80d8a4693936543cc866/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L129)) accepts only a power after a text group, so `/ \mathrm{s}` is not a unit tail. The group must then read as a symbol, which L130-L136 allow only for a one-token group that starts a term, touches the previous token or is one upright letter. So `\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}` and `215 \, \text{kJ}/\text{mol}` are rejected, and `30 \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}` parses as `30 m/s`.
- Ordinals: the group in `11^{\text{th}}` follows `{`, so the start-of-term rule ([L134](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e3de9706b774c02117ec80d8a4693936543cc866/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L134)) reads `th` as a symbol and the reference parses as `11^th`.
- Powers: `TERMINAL_UNIT_POWER` ([L68](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e3de9706b774c02117ec80d8a4693936543cc866/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L68)) allows neither a sign nor spaces inside the braces.

Reproduce with `uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra math python repro.py`:

```python
from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
from verifyit.spec import MathSpec

for reference, value in [(r"30 \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}", "30"), (r"11^{\text{th}}", "11"), (r"9.9 \, \text{s}^{-1}", "9.9")]:
    try:
        print(reference, grade_math_candidate(MathSpec(expected=reference), value).reward)
    except Exception as error:
        print(reference, type(error).__name__)
```

On e3de9706b it prints `0.0`, `0.0` and `InvalidTask`; on 0c236d36c it prints `1.0` three times.

Expected: each reference gives 1 to its value and 0 to a wrong value, as before #11989.

I have a tested patch that restores 26 of the 27 rows (all but `1000 \, \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{s}`) and changes no other row of the census, with regression tests; I can open it as a PR.

diagnostics.title: [evals][eval_policy] Eval Policy Changes for Nov 30 Update
diagnostics.body:
We are targeting an update to our post-training eval policy on November 30th, 2026\. The new policy will focus on improving coverage over key capabilities, especially factuality and math/science reasoning. The purpose of this issue is to invite the community to provide feedback on the listed evals and suggest changes to our implementations.

## Changes to In-Distribution Benchmarks

The tables below list the major changes to our the in-distribution benchmark composition.

* Benchmarks slated for **removal** will be taken out of the policy with high probability,
* Benchmarks flagged for **changes** need some repair to make them work on more recent versions of main,  
* Benchmarks marked as **potential additions** have draft implementations and may be included in the next round.

We will select our in-distribution benchmarks to collectively cover the capabilities necessary for Mochi to do well on our out-of-distribution benchmarks (listed below). Beginning in 2027, we hope to make this process more data-driven, but for the Nov 30 policy, we will select ID benchmarks based on:

1. Our assessment of each benchmark’s quality and appropriateness for hillclimbing,  
2. Whether an eval can be run reliably in our eval infrastructure,  
3. The resource cost of running the eval,  
4. The wall clock time of running the eval,  
5. Coverage over our out-of-distribution benchmarks,  
6. Whether we find eval contamination in our training data.

In the policy announcement on Nov 30, we will explain why particular evaluations were included or excluded. Our full set of in-distribution evals must run in no more than 24 hours for Mochi, and our eval lite subset used for model development must run in no more than 3 hours.

The proposed changes favor more recent evaluations (which have a smaller chance of contamination and reflect modern capability priorities) while increasing implicit weight on scientific tasks. This includes the addition of a number of benchmarks specifically targeting scientific knowledge and reasoning. New core capability benchmarks target factuality (SimpleQA Verified, FACTS Parametric/Grounding), instruction following (MultiChallenge) and realistic long context tasks (LongBench v2). We have not significantly changed the set of agentic evaluations in this round and will instead focus on reliable, performant implementations of our existing evals, with a few exceptions.

diagnostics.title: [long-loop] Ablate the RL optimizer and learning rate for Mochi and Snowball
diagnostics.body:
Mochi and Snowball long-loop RL need an ablated optimizer and learning rate. Since the 2026-11-23 normalization, both models use MuonH with `lr` 1e-5 and `adam_lr` 2.307692307692308e-6 (`offload_momentum: true`), `max_grad_norm` 0.5 and 64 prompts × 8 samples per batch. Snowball moved from AdamW to MuonH for memory: AdamW state did not fit at long context without CPU optimizer offload, and offload slowed each step. Neither the optimizer nor the learning rate came from an ablation. The earlier tuned Snowball RL comparison in #7786 (hypothesis V) found that AdamW learned faster and reached a higher peak training reward than MuonH. This experiment should settle both choices for each model. It is planned here and not yet scheduled.

Design:
- Curriculum: our best RL curriculum at the time it runs, identical for both models. Record its identity and version.
- Fixed settings: the normalized config for all other settings (staleness 3, 98,304-token response cap and 131,072-token context, batch 64 × 8, `max_grad_norm` 0.5), one seed per arm, and the frozen 200-row validation split from the curriculum.
- Optimizer arms: (a) MuonH with `offload_momentum: true` and the `adam_lr`/`lr` ratio held fixed; (b) AdamW with CPU optimizer offload. Each arm uses the qualified trainer layout for its memory profile.
- Grid per optimizer and model: half-decade steps. MuonH starts at 3e-6, 1e-5, 3e-5 and 1e-4. AdamW starts at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5. Learning rates do not transfer between optimizers.
- Metric: an EMA of validation accuracy over the first 20 optimizer updates (EMA window 5, matching best-checkpoint selection). Report raw per-eval accuracy and training reward alongside it.
- Cost: report median seconds per update and GPU-hours per update for each arm, split into rollout wait, optimizer step and offload transfer. AdamW with offload wins only if its accuracy gain justifies its step-time cost.
- Adaptive grid: if the best arm of an optimizer is at either edge of its grid, add the next half-decade step beyond that edge and repeat until the best value is interior.
- Stability checks per arm: training/inference mismatch KL, gradient norm and the clipped-gradient fraction. Report any divergence as a result, not a rerun.

Done when:
- Each optimizer has a learning-rate curve per model whose best value is interior to its grid, with EMA validation accuracy at 20 updates and seconds per update per arm.
- A recommended optimizer and learning rate per model is stated, with the accuracy, cost and stability metrics that support it.
- The long-loop RL defaults are updated, or confirmed unchanged, from that recommendation.

🤖 # Research

This issue requires two new model evaluations and a calibrated plot estimate; no result or overlapping PR is linked to #12173. The [preserved document-loss scorer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/snowball_uncheatable_losses.py#L127-L181) already sums token loss and source bytes for BPB, and its [July manifest config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/configs/snowball_history_20260909/cooldown-42150.json) pins the requested dataset revision. Its [loader and tokenizer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/snowball-document-losses-2026-09-16/experiments/evaluation/snowball_uncheatable_losses.py#L339-L393) are Snowball specific; Levanter's aggregate BPB has separate known errors in [#10968](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10968).

# Proposed Fix

1. Check the pinned July manifest against Hugging Face revision `65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545`; select the same 500 C++ and 500 Python documents for both models, recording IDs, text hashes, and byte counts. Keep evaluation data, checkpoint caches, and outputs in the execution region.
2. Validate a document scorer for the released Mochi step 393,491 and Gemma 4 31B base at the checkpoint revisions in this issue. Use each native tokenizer and 4,096-token windows; on a small diagnostic sample, check checkpoint loading, one count per predicted token, exclusion of auxiliary loss, and UTF-8 source-byte denominators. Adapt the preserved scorer only where the model loaders require it, then run both full evaluations on Iris and retain job links, configs, code revision, precision, and per-document exports.
3. For each model and language, compute BPB as `sum(token NLL) / (ln(2) × sum(source UTF-8 bytes))`; require 500 unique, finite records per language and report exclusions if any. Give C++ and Python equal weight for the model comparison. Compare Gemma's measured values with the published 0.25293 C++ and 0.33209 Python, including absolute and percentage differences.
4. Recover the DeepSeek V4 Pro Base and Kimi K2 Base reference coordinates from the [original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972). Report Mochi's coordinate from the two-anchor mapping and from a fit that includes Gemma, with the numerical shift between them. State that Gemma's plot height is inferred and that mapping July code BPB to the plot's evaluation data adds uncertainty; use the older-to-July holdout errors already recorded in this issue as a sensitivity check.

If model support requires a code change, link its PR with `Part of #12173`; the final results should be recorded on this issue before it closes.

🤖 The 0.879 coordinate uses chart heights for Kimi K2 Base (in both fits) and Gemma 4 31B (in the three-anchor fit). Neither model is in the MAI report linked above or on Elie's chart. Where do those two heights come from?

[Figure 1 of the MAI report](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf) gives code bits per byte (BPB) on MAI's codebase for six models: MAI-Base-1 0.2401, MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL 0.2446, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B 0.2400, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base 0.2370, Kimi K3 0.2264 and MAI-Base-2 0.2203. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base is the only outside base model, and the Kimi entry is the post-trained K3. Elie's chart converts these values with the MAI-Base-1/MAI-Base-2 line in step 3 below, which puts DeepSeek at 0.869 and Kimi K3 at 0.837. On the July C++/Python mean, Mochi (0.2577) sits 49.6% of the way from DeepSeek (0.2476) to Kimi K2 Base (0.2680, from #8824). The two-anchor 0.8788 therefore needs a Kimi K2 Base height of 0.889, which matches no Kimi point on the chart. If the Kimi K2 and Gemma heights were derived from DeepSeek and an assumed slope, the fit has one measured anchor. The 0.0103 chart-unit miss for held-out Gemma would then test that derivation. It would not test the mapping to OpenAI's evaluation.

We propose calibrating our code BPB directly against MAI's, using the four Figure 1 models with public weights. The report says only post-trained checkpoints of Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 and MiMo are available, so MAI scored the same weights we can download.

| Model | Active / total parameters (Figure 1) | MAI code BPB | July C++/Python mean BPB |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base | 49B / 1.6T | 0.2370 | 0.2476 (#8824) |
| Kimi K3, post-trained | 104B / 2.8T | 0.2264 | not scored |
| Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, post-trained | 95B / 2.4T | 0.2400 | not scored |
| MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL, post-trained | 42B / 1.02T | 0.2446 | not scored |

1. Score all four models and Mochi on the screened October split above (470 C++ and 490 Python files), with the scorer used here for Mochi and Gemma. Qwen3.8 and MiMo were released on August 8 and September 21, after the July files, so their training data may contain those files. All four were released before the October files were pushed, and the October screen already removed files that overlap Mochi's training data.
2. Fit MAI code BPB against our October BPB across the four models. Report the slope, the residuals and the leave-one-out errors.
3. Apply the fit to Mochi's October BPB, then map the result to the chart through MAI-Base-1 (0.2401 at 0.878) and MAI-Base-2 (0.2203 at 0.819): chart = 0.878 + 2.98 × (MAI BPB − 0.2401).

Each anchor in this chain is measured on both of the scales it connects. The chain still assumes a linear map from our code files to MAI's codebase, that post-trained checkpoints follow the same line as base models, and the MAI-Base-1/MAI-Base-2 line.

Expect large residuals. Across the 13 open base models in #8824, regressing the July C++/Python mean on Paloma's 100-language code subset leaves a residual standard deviation of 0.027 BPB (R² 0.54). If the MAI fit scatters that much, the chart coordinate carries about ±0.08 (0.027 × 2.98). The code set also matters. Mochi's BPB is 4.1% above DeepSeek's on the July C++/Python mean and 18.5% above on Paloma's code subset. At 1.79 chart units per BPB of gap from DeepSeek (2.98 × 0.60, the central slope on Elie's chart), that difference moves Mochi from 0.887 to 0.944.

@Calvin-Xu, we tested your loss-to-loss idea on newer UncheatableEval files. **A straight line captures a trend, with substantial scatter.** Using all 8 completed comparison models in one fit, final Mochi (step 393,491) lands at **0.243 ± 0.007 bits per byte on MAI code** and **0.888 ± 0.020 on Elie’s OpenAI log-perplexity axis**.

### What changed in the eval?

We switched from July after finding training code in 19 of its scored files. We screened the official October split against 16.643B tokens actually consumed during Mochi training. Of 1,000 candidate code files, we removed 21 with independently verified code matches and 19 more in the vendored/generated and near-duplicate screen. The audit covers a sample of Mochi’s training stream, so residual overlap is possible. [Pinned October dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-10/tree/87a300906c15c2433c5285035042dabdcbec0725)

Every model saw the same **470 C++ and 490 Python files**. We scored the observed tokens in 4,096-token windows, summed their loss per language, and divided by UTF-8 bytes. Giving the two languages equal weight yields **0.28696 bits per byte for Mochi**, directly measured on the public files.

### Does a straight line predict MAI code loss?

The plot pairs each model’s measured public-code loss with its published MAI code loss. To put both reports on the MAI-2 scale, we kept the MAI-1 report’s model-to-model differences and shifted its values by −0.0040 BPB, the change in their common MAI-Base-1 reference. Mochi’s public score falls inside the calibration range. [MAI-1 Figure 10](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf#page=24) · [MAI-2 Figure 1](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/Frontier-Pre-training-at-Microsoft-AI.pdf)

![The 8 measured model coordinates and fitted straight line relating public code loss to MAI code loss.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/mai-code-transfer-8.png)

The fit explains **69%** of the variation among these points. We also hid each entire model family, refitted on the others, and predicted the hidden scores. The resulting prediction error was **0.0068 BPB**. Each family contributes equally to the RMSE. That small set of families supports using a line for interpolation and leaves considerable uncertainty for a new family such as Mochi.

### How does Mochi score on the public files?

![Direct C++ and Python bits per byte for final Mochi and all completed comparison models.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/october-code-scores-8.png)

Additional direct measurements on the same files, averaged over the two languages, are Inkling 2 Mini **0.27889**, Inkling 2 Small **0.22817**, Reflection Beam 1.0 (instruction-tuned BF16) **0.24964** BPB. These checkpoints have no published MAI code score in the two reports, so the calibration still uses 8 models. For these checkpoints and MiMo, the scorer uses EOS before the first source token because the checkpoints have no declared BOS. [Comparison weights and per-language scores](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/additional-comparisons.json)

**Inkling 2 Mini versus Mochi.** Mini loses on C++ by 0.0158 BPB and wins on Python by 0.0320. With equal language weights, Mini averages 0.2789 to Mochi’s 0.2870, a 2.8% lower loss. Its advantage is 0.0081 BPB (95% paired file-bootstrap interval 0.0047–0.0113, resampling within each language). We screened overlap against Mochi’s training stream. Inkling’s training exposure to these files is unknown. [Paired results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/paired-extra-vs-mochi.json)

### Where does that put Mochi on Elie’s plot?

We mapped the predicted MAI code BPB through Elie’s MAI-1/MAI-2 calibration, using `0.878 + 2.98 × (MAI code BPB − 0.2401)`. Scaling the family-held-out RMSE by the same factor gives the transfer error quoted above. Uncertainty in the two-point OpenAI mapping is additional. OpenAI’s private evaluation remains unmeasured for Mochi. [Elie’s original plot](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2124686143165734972) · [Numerical results](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WhenWen/marin/7dc3f5237c1924653d199600307b963bda328545/reports/mochi-base-log-perplexity/october-calibration/mai-code-transfer-8.json)

Kimi K3.1 Pro occupies the original Kimi proxy’s horizontal position. Its label names the released checkpoint we scored. GLM-5.3 uses its official `[gMASK]<sop>` start and lands at 0.877. 🤖 **Scale difference from Exp1–Exp4 and Arm 1 dependency**

## Scale comparison

Our one-at-a-time SFT ablations run at 1/8th the per-update batch size of Exp1–Exp4:

| Setting | Exp1–Exp4 runs | Our 64-H100 ablations |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | 32 hosts × 8 H100 (256 H100 in Exp1) | 8 hosts × 8 H100 (64 H100; mesh `context=8`, `data=8`) |
| Packed rows per update | 256 (`256 × 262,144` = 67,108,864 tokens) | 32 (`trainer.trainer.train_batch_size: 32`; `32 × 262,144` = 8,388,608 tokens, 1/8×) |
| Microbatch / accumulation | — | `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` (4 microbatches of 8 rows scanned inside one update; loss divided by the full 32-row scored-token count, `_accumulated_loss_and_grads` at commit `3b291b10`) |
| Updates per run (`stop_after_steps`) | 204 (Exp2), 360 (Exp4), 388 (Exp3), 746 (Exp1) | 150 (one-hour size); 500 (8-hour size) |
| Raw tokens per run | 13.69 B (204 updates) to 50.06 B (746 updates) | 1.26 B (150 updates, 4,800 rows); 4.19 B (500 updates, 16,000 rows) |

Because both batch size per update (8×) and total trained tokens are smaller than Exp1–Exp4, effects that depend on batch size or longer training horizons may differ between the one-hour screen, the 8-hour screen, and 256-H100 scale.

## Arm 1 dependency

Arm 1 (changing stored parameter precision from BF16 to FP32 under Exp1's optimizer routing, with 4-D routed expert banks on Adam and stacked norm scales on Muon-H) waits on issue 11793 (first-update hang under that combination on the current long-loop runtime). Isolating optimizer routing on FP32 likewise waits on issue 11793, while the BF16 single-knob arms and an FP32 combined precision-plus-routing check do not hit issue 11793.

🤖

## Research

This is a multi-run experiment with no results yet. The historical comparison also changes RL duration (16 versus 36 updates), so SFT-only scores cannot by themselves explain the post-RL gap. [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) documents the BF16 stored-parameter caveat in the Exp1-style baseline; [#11793](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) blocks the FP32 plus Exp1-routing comparison on the current runtime. The Exp3/Exp4 supervision sidecar is hash-pinned in [`exp3_recipe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1be0454367925411db6a432da3f62901881f8152/experiments/post_training/long_loop/exp3_recipe.py#L114-L126), but its per-source loss modes still need to be checked against the intended mask arm.

## Plan

1. Freeze the pre-train checkpoint, 10/05 catalog, source-loss sidecar and hash, runtime revision, data order, update count, and evaluation policy. Inspect the sidecar's per-source modes and verify that each arm changes only its named setting. Split the proposed LR/betas/eps and packing-cap/lookahead arms; separate expert-bank and norm routing if those assignments can be varied independently.
2. Run a matched Exp1-style BF16 baseline and one-hour SFT screens with the same source weights, sampling seed, update count, and checkpoint steps. Record consumed token counts because packing and masking change them. Score each checkpoint on the same frozen Micro210 and edit-call evaluations. Repeat the baseline to measure run and evaluation variation before promoting an arm whose score change exceeds that spread.
3. Keep the FP32 plus Exp1-routing cell gated on #11793. Once update 1 completes reliably, run a matched precision × routing comparison, then take only the decisive settings to eight-hour, repeated SFT runs. Report both Micro aggregates, benchmark-level scores, coverage, edit-call scores, seeds, configs, and checkpoint links, including negative results.
4. For any SFT setting that plausibly explains the gap, continue a matched pair through the same RL recipe and number of updates. Compare the post-RL checkpoints under one evaluation policy before attributing any part of the Exp1-to-Exp4 post-RL difference to SFT.

🤖 **Optimizer routing per recipe: Exp1's expert banks fall through to Adam**

Source-verified parameter routing across five recipes (Exp1, Exp2, Exp3/Exp4 Hero-EP, the 11-19 control at `6164fcbd`, and the 10/05 run). No claim is made here about which routing performs better.

Conventions used below: `learning_rate` drives Muon-H and AdamH; `adam_lr` drives Adam. "Per-group" clip means `max_grad_norm` applied separately inside each optimizer group; "Global" means one gradient-norm clip across all parameters.

## Cross-recipe overview

| Weight group | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`, `bcf85728`) | Exp3 / Exp4 (`facbad18`) & 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`, `1f9bb1af`) | Real 10/05 (`ce7c77a`, `11baea1f`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`, `AdamConfig`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert banks (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`)** | **Adam** (4-D fall-through) | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Attention & shared-expert matrices | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Gated norms | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` | **Muon-H** (2-D match; no norm rule) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `embed_norm` / `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `output_proj` / LM head | AdamH | AdamH | AdamH | Adam |
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| Clipping | none | global 1.0 | none | global 1.0 |

Every recipe except Exp2 uses mixed routing, with `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate`, and `output_proj` routed the same way across all mixed recipes; Exp2 is the only recipe applying plain Adam uniformly to all parameters.

## Per-recipe routing tables (verified from source)

### (a) Exp1 (`9662fdba02`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `bcf85728`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:285-307`. The SFT runtime stacks transformer blocks (`Transformer.stacked_blocks: ArrayStacked[Block]`, `sft_runtime/model.py:1251, 1283`), turning `(E, D, I)` expert weights (`levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:389-392`) into 4-D `(L, E, D, I)` leaves.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam (`L291-297`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` (LM head) | AdamH (`L298-299`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| gated norms (`embed`, `attn`, `mlp`, `final`) | Muon-H (`L301-302`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| attention `w_q/k/v/o`, shared expert `w_*`, latent `w_*` (stacked 3-D) | Muon-H (`L303-304`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| **expert banks `w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down` (4-D)** | **Adam** (`L305` fall-through) | **`adam_lr`** | none |
| stacked RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` (2-D) | **Muon-H** (`L303-304`; no norm rule in this blob) | `learning_rate` | none |
| `embed_norm` and `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam (`L305`) | `adam_lr` | none |

`max_grad_norm: null` (`sft.yaml:75`) and blob `bcf85728` has no global clip option. Both `learning_rate` and `adam_lr` are `5e-5` (`sft.yaml:61, 73`), so the Adam fall-through changed the update rule for expert banks without changing their LR value.

### (b) Exp3 / Exp4 Hero-EP (blob `facbad18`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_hero_ep_muonh_v1`; mask at `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:308-327`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L314-315`) | `adam_lr = 5e-5 * 3/13 = 1.1538e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L316-317`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L319-320`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| any `.weight` (RMSNorm scales, ShortConv) | Adam (`L323-324`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| expert banks (4-D) and other 2/3-D matrices | Muon-H (`L325-326`; normalised per expert bank via `expert_normalization`, `L86-92`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Per-group `max_grad_norm` is `None`. Global `1.0` clipping is set outside the optimizer (`global_gradient_clip=1`, `exp3_recipe:138`) and applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`.

### (c) 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `1f9bb1af`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:339-363`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L345-351`) | `adam_lr` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L352-353`) | `learning_rate` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L355-356`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| `.weight` (norm scales) | Adam (`L357-358`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. expert banks | Muon-H (`L359-360`; 4-D banks use the hero backend with `expert_normalization: all_experts`, `use_syrk: true`, build `L263-297`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Clipping comes from `global_grad_norm: 1.0` applied once before all groups (`L329-337`); per-group `max_grad_norm` is `null`. Routing matches Hero-EP `(b)`, and both use `expert_normalization: all_experts` and `use_syrk: true` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:228, 230` defaults in Exp3/Exp4); they differ in LRs (`learning_rate` `2e-5` vs `5e-5`; `adam_lr` `2e-5` vs `1.1538e-5`), with `1f9bb1af` sending 4-D leaves through the hero backend and 2/3-D leaves through the generic backend.

### (d) Real 10/05 run (`ce7c77a`, HF model card revision `8c76b22a`)

Trainer `experiments/grug_sft/special_token_lr.py` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True` at `L334`); optimizer `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py` `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (blob `11baea1f`, not `bcf85728`).

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L306-312`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L313-314`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales | Adam (`L317-318`, `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) | `adam_lr` | none |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L320-321`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. **expert banks** | **Muon-H** (`L328-329`) | `learning_rate` | none |

Config sets `learning_rate=5e-5`, `adam_lr=5e-5`, `max_grad_norm=None` (`special_token_lr.py:361-373`) with no global clip. One extra rule scales updates to the 7 special-token rows of `token_embed` and `output_proj` by `×√32` after the optimizer (`special_token_train.py:498-505`).

### (e) Exp2 (`442bf9d878`)

Plain Levanter `AdamConfig` (`levanter/optim/config.py:503-535`) with a single group (no mask, no `multi_transform`): every parameter gets `clip_by_global_norm(1.0)`, then `scale_by_adam`, then `lr = 5e-5`. Weight decay is `0`, so the decay mask is unused.

## Evidence that Exp1's 4-D expert-bank fall-through was unintended

- **Docstring mismatch:** The same blob `bcf85728` lists `"MoE MLP"` under `muonh` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:215`).
- **`(2, 3)` rule vs. stacked 4-D banks:** The `ndim in (2, 3)` rule was written for the `grug/moe` template (`grug/moe/model.py`, `blocks: tuple[Block, ...]`), where expert weights are 3-D and match Muon-H. `sft_runtime/model.py` stacks blocks into `ArrayStacked[Block]`, making expert banks 4-D, and the mask in `bcf85728` was not updated for 4-D leaves.
- **Explicit 10/05 comment:** The 10/05 optimizer (`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py:322-327`, blob `11baea1f`) explicitly guards against this trap: *"plus 4D when use_array_stacked_blocks=True… Without including 4D, stacked expert weights fall through to adam"*.
- **Branch fix not in `main`:** Commit `02c96d8378` (2026-11-17, `"[grug] Preserve Muon state across expert routing"`, no commit message body) adds 4-D routing, the `.weight` → Adam rule, and `test_muonh_groups_match_hero_for_stacked_and_unstacked_models`. It is present in `6164fcbd` but **not in `main`**.
- **Still in `origin/main`:** `origin/main` (blob `81304114`, `L311`) still checks `ndim in (2, 3)`, so any stacked-block run on `main` using `grug_moe_muonh_v1` repeats Exp1's routing (which current recipes on `main` use it was not checked).
- Nothing found in source records the Exp1 fall-through routing as a deliberate choice.

## What Exp1 → Exp3 changed in optimizer routing

Moving from Exp1 (`bcf85728`) to Exp3 (`facbad18`) changed three optimizer behaviors together:

1. **Expert banks (`w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down`):** Adam → Muon-H (with per-expert-bank `expert_normalization`).
2. **Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)`:** Muon-H → Adam (via the `.weight` rule, and at `adam_lr = 1.1538e-5` instead of `5e-5`).
3. **Gradient clipping:** none → global norm clip `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1` in `exp3_recipe:138`, applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`).

## Unverified detail

How generic Muon (`_grug_scale_with_muon`) handles Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales was **not traced or verified**. As a 2-D leaf they may be orthogonalised across layers as a single matrix, so that behavior is left open rather than stated as fact.

## Open question for experiment owners

Was Adam on the 4-D expert banks (and Muon-H on stacked RMSNorm scales) in Exp1 intended, or an unintended result of stacking blocks under the `ndim in (2, 3)` rule?

🤖

| updates with a pre-clip total grad norm above 1.0 | 17 of 150 (updates 1-10, 13, 28, 31, 71, 101, 117, 144) | 18 of 150 |

- **How clipping works here:** the optimizer (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`) clips each of its three parameter groups to norm 1.0 separately, not the total norm. In the step-150 checkpoint manifest (`opt_state`), the groups hold these parameters: AdamH holds `output_proj`; Adam holds `token_embed`, `embed_norm`, `final_norm`, the routers, router bias, attention gates and the expert MLPs (`expert_mlp` w_gate and w_up stored as `[26, 256, 2560, 1280]`, w_down as `[26, 256, 1280, 2560]`); MuonH holds the other matrices, the gated norms and the stacked `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp` weights (stored as `[26, 2560]`). So the binding count uses the group norms. In the clip run, the MuonH group was above 1.0 on 8 updates, AdamH on 13 and Adam on none. Nearly all of it is the first 13 updates plus 4 later spikes.
- **Where the numbers come from:** W&B logs `grad/norm/<parameter>` before the optimizer, so these are pre-clip norms. Each group norm is rebuilt from the 27 logged per-parameter norms, using the optimizer's own grouping rule. Their sum of squares matches the logged `grad/norm/total` within 1% on every update.

  - Clipping can act from update 2 on. Mean absolute gap over updates 2-150 is 0.00034, and 12 updates differ by more than 0.001. The largest gap is 0.0044, at update 79, where the no-clip run had its one large spike (MuonH group norm 9.00 and Adam group norm 1.50, against 0.23 and 0.06 in the clip run).

🤖 Arm F splits the two ways Adam differs from Muon-H on the banks. It keeps the per-coordinate normalization and drops the momentum, and it lands with arm E: Micro210 49.57% against 50.19%, +22.81 and +23.42 pp over the matched control. Its SFT loss sits between the two (0.536 against 0.488 for arm E and 0.648 for the control), so momentum may add a little, but most of the gain comes without it. That leaves the size of the step.

At the same rate the two kinds of rule take very different steps on a bank. Adam and the RMS rule scale each coordinate by the running RMS of its own gradient, so one update moves each coordinate by up to about the rate, 2e-5. Muon-H's hyperball update moves a bank by the rate times its Frobenius norm, which is 2e-5 × RMS(W) per coordinate. In the public long-loop base (`open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`) the routed experts have RMS(W) = 0.00975, so if the banks these arms start from are of that scale, the Muon-H step is about 100 times smaller per coordinate, and 150 updates move a bank by at most 0.3% of its norm. Exp1's Adam-updated banks show the full-size steps: on values below 2^-9, where BF16 rounding does not interfere, their RMS change is 1.34e-3, and 746 full-size steps of 5e-5 with uncorrelated signs give 5e-5 × √746 = 1.37e-3.

If the step size is the cause, Muon-H banks with a bank-only rate near 2e-5 / 0.00975 ≈ 2e-3 should close most of the gap. One more one-hour arm like E and F would test it, and would show whether the banks need a different rule or only a larger step.

## Mochi Bank-RMS probes: the line stops

We ran short probes of the RMSProp-style expert-bank rule on Mochi. The rule keeps a second moment only and has no momentum. Each probe restored Mochi's step-400407 SFT checkpoint and ran 20 updates (400407..400426). The reference twin is the production Muon-H run from the same checkpoint. All runs share update 400407, so the means below cover the 19 updates after it (400408..400426).

The rule was written before the last probe ran: mean loss within 1.05x of the twin, and no grad norm above 5.

| probe | mean loss, 400408..400426 | ratio to twin | grad norm | written rule |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Twin (Muon-H, production) | 0.483053 | 1.000 | 0.35 to 1.26 | reference |
| Control v2 (Muon-H banks, probe commit) | 0.483036 | 1.000 | max 0.737 | pass |
| Bank-RMS, cold start (bank state zero, full LR) | 0.828535 | 1.715 | 218.67 at 400413 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment (20 warm-up passes, full LR) | 0.629574 | 1.303 | 136.21 at 400415 | fail |
| Bank-RMS, warm second moment, 0.25x bank LR | 0.521396 | 1.079 | 10.44 at 400409, 5.88 at 400413 | fail |

## What the probes show

- **Code ruled out.** Control v2 ran the same commit as the cold probe, with Muon-H on the banks. It matched the twin (1.000x, no spike at 400413). So the gap in the cold probe comes from the bank rule with fresh state, not from the newer code base.
- **The cold start is not the main cause.** Warming the second moment removed the 400413 spike (loss 0.667 against 3.711 cold). Most of the gap stayed: 1.29x the twin without 400413, against 1.38x cold.
- **Warm start plus a 0.25x bank LR is still 1.079x the twin and unstable.** All 19 updates are above the twin (1.014x to 1.261x per update). The grad norm passes 5 twice.
- **Snowball is not a like-for-like guide.** In Snowball, the bank arms were ahead of their own controls from update 1 (loss ratio 0.984 at update 1 in all three pairs). Their mean loss ratios over updates 2..20 were 0.913, 0.954 and 0.922; the one with the same RMSProp-style rule was 0.954. But each Snowball pair is two cold starts from the pre-train base with every optimizer slot fresh. Mochi sets a fresh bank state against a warm Muon-H twin mid-schedule.

## Decision

- Under the written rule, the Mochi Bank-RMS line stops here. There will be no 8-hour Mochi Bank-RMS run.
- A like-for-like test would need a fresh-optimizer start from Mochi's pre-train base.

Two more 8-hour runs (500 updates, step 500, trained and scored on cw-rno2a) with expert banks on Adam (arm E): **P2** repeats arm E r2 at trainer seed 2, and **P3** is arm E with 10% pretraining replay instead of 20.47% (seed 0). They are compared with **arm E r2** (seed 0, 20.47%), the **20.47% control** (Muon-H on every matrix, seed 0) and the **plain 10% replay run** (19 Nov recipe, expert banks on Muon-H; a different recipe and code commit).

- **Held-out loss (step 500):** P2's SFT loss is 0.4425, against 0.4488 for arm E r2 and 0.5413 for the control; P3's is 0.4247. P2 is 0.0988 and P3 is 0.1166 below the control. Pretrain macro loss is 0.8599 (P2), 0.8613 (P3), 0.8589 (arm E r2) and 0.8515 (control).
- **Edit-call:** every P2 and P3 interval overlaps arm E r2's and the control's. Pooled applied edits: P2 0.782, P3 0.768, arm E r2 0.825, control 0.765. P3 is below arm E r2 on all ten rates.
- **Micro210** (14 clean sources, two repeats): P2 50.56% and P3 51.60%, against 57.70% for arm E r2 and 45.18% for the control. Both P2 repeats and both P3 repeats are below both arm E r2 repeats and above both control repeats.

**Across the three measures:** the three Adam-bank runs (arm E r2 at seed 0 and 20.47%, P2 at seed 2 and 20.47%, P3 at seed 0 and 10%) each have lower held-out SFT loss and higher Micro210 than the control, while P2's and P3's edit-call intervals overlap the control's. Arm E r2 scored 7.13 pp above P2 (the same recipe at another seed, which also changes the data order) and 6.10 pp above P3 on equal-weight Micro210, so a single arm E run can sit several points away from another on Micro210. One training run per configuration; no causal claim.
